title: Chapter 78 – Blind
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

On the first morning, he drops the pestle.

It is a small thing. A stone pestle, the weight of a loaf, that he has lifted ten thousand times since the Register. He has it in his right hand over the mortar in the Pill Hall yard, grinding bark, and it slips. It hits the rim and cracks across and falls in two pieces to the flagstones with a sound like a shot.

Every head in the courtyard turns.

"Lin Jian," says Steward Gu.

"I am sorry, Steward. My hand was wet."

"Your hand is shaking."

He looks at it. It is. A fine fast tremor runs along the fingers and into the wrist, as regular as a struck string. He closes the hand into a fist and holds it against his thigh until the tremor stops, and says, "It is cold, Steward. I did not sleep."

"The Pill Hall pays for pestles," says Gu, to the floor. "You will pay for this one in the third week of the month." He bends, with a grunt, and picks up the pieces. His small bright eyes come up and pass over Jian's face once, sharply, and drop again. "Go and sit by the furnace. You are the color of tallow."

Jian sits. He puts his back to the warm bronze flank of furnace nine and shuts his eyes.

The gray line is still in the corner of his sight. Booting. Fragment 3 not found. Searching. It has not changed since the landing. It does not flicker or fade. Beneath it, if he looks for it, there is now a second, smaller line, in the same pale ash color.

```
Day 1 of 30.
```

Thirty. He counts them off, slowly, as a prisoner counts bars. Twenty-nine more mornings like this one. Twenty-nine more days in which he will look at a stone and see only a stone, at a man and see only a man, at a herb and not know its grade. It is not the loss of power that frightens him. He has lost power before; he lost it in the Garden, in the forge, on the road. It is the loss of a sense. His mind keeps reaching for it. It reaches the way a tongue goes to the gap of a pulled tooth.

I did not know how much I leaned on it.

He had not known how much of his thinking was done in the presence of the thing. When he looked at a furnace he had read the heat; he had thought the reading was his own. When he looked at a person he had read their Qi, and the reading had come so smoothly that it felt like instinct. Now there is only what the eye gives him. Skin, cloth, a shadow. It is like waking on the first morning of this life, in a strange body, with no idea of the room.

Thirty days.

He opens his eyes. The courtyard is full of boys at furnaces. Hua Ning stands at number four with her arms folded, watching him with her flat dislike. Cai, beside her, is looking at the sky. Nobody knows. That, at least, is the same as it was.

Be a youth of twenty-one who has not slept.

He gets up and goes back to the bench.

* * *

Elder Duan's inspection of the fortieth landing takes a day and a half, and finds nothing.

Jian hears it from Ma Bao, who hears it from his cousin, who is a servant in the Enforcement Hall's kitchens. The stonecutters came at dawn with chisels and picks. They lifted the disk from its post and set it on a cloth. They sounded the paving with iron rods. They sent a boy down the shaft where the post is sunk, with a lamp on a string, and the boy came up and said there was nothing in it but gravel. The array was tested at every landing by three Foundation cultivators, one after another, and each of them said it was in perfect order.

"They think the reading was a fault," says Ma Bao, ladling millet in the refectory. "Old stone. Cracks in the jade. Duan said, Four hundred years. Then he said replace the post." He sounds almost disappointed. "They will cut a new one in the spring."

"And Keeper Fu?"

"Retired." Ma Bao shrugs. "That is what my cousin says. Retired, and sent to the Library. He has been a keeper for forty years. They gave him a cup."

Jian eats. The millet is hot and tasteless. He thinks of the old man's pale eyes, the other book that no one is shown. In case it is explained later.

He thinks: They took the book. And they took Fu with it. And whatever it said, Duan has read.

"They are going to put a guard on the stair," adds Ma Bao, scraping his bowl. "At night. Two of the inner disciples, in rotation. The first-ranker has been stood down." He looks at Jian with sly sympathy. "Your brother is furious."

"Is he?"

"He said he never wanted the duty." Ma Bao grins. "He said it twice."

He is not furious, thinks Jian. He is protecting me. It takes him a moment to see how: a first-ranker who is angry at losing a duty is a first-ranker who was never there at the third watch.

He puts down his spoon.

"I am going to see how the Medicine Valley looks in the snow," he says.

* * *

The pot is gone from the foot of the pine on Terrace Nine.

He had not expected it to be there. He had expected, if anything, a message. But he stands in the new snow with his hands in his sleeves and looks at the exact spot where he set the clay down, and it is bare earth, scuffed, with a pale ring where the pot sat. Nothing else. No footprints. The snow has covered them.

He squats. He brushes the dirt with his fingers.

There is a smear on the root. It is thin and dark and glossy, no longer than a grain of rice. It has dried to the color of rust. He touches it with the tip of a finger and smells the finger.

Iron.

He found it. He took it. He left his mark. There is no panel to tell him what it means, no gray line to read the Qi on the bark, no soft cold voice in his head to say residue. There is only a smear, and a smell, and his own judgment, which is a thing he has to learn to trust again.

He has sent me a reply. It says: I was here.

He stays squatting for a long time, with the flakes settling on his shoulders. Below, across the roofs, the bell of the Contribution Hall tolls the noon, and on the second terrace the furnaces smoke. A woman's laughter drifts up from the laundry. The world is very ordinary.

And I cannot see him.

For the first time since he stepped through the Gate, he is afraid, and the fear is not the sharp bright fear of a fight. It is the dull slow fear of a man in a dark room who has heard a floorboard.

* * *

Pebble wakes on the third night.

He feels it before he hears it, the small dry scrabble of claws against the lining of the beast bag. It is the middle of the night. The courtyard is dark and cold. He sits up on his cot and slips the bag out from under his blanket and unties the neck with fingers that, he notes, are steady.

A nose comes out first. It is small and damp and a little crooked. Then a head, covered in tiny bronze scales, with two bright black eyes. Then a body, the length of his forearm, plated like an artichoke, curled into itself, trembling.

Hello, he thinks, and does not say it.

Pebble regards him in the dark. A wash of feeling comes up through the bond, warm and a little reproachful: hunger, cold, the vague indignation of a creature who has been put in a sack and not told why. Under it is something else. A fine thin thread of attention, wound round a spot on Jian's chest, just below the breastbone, where the Interface used to sit.

It is looking for it.

It is not there, he thinks. I am sorry.

The thread draws tight, then slackens. The pangolin makes a small, offended noise and climbs, with infinite deliberation, up his arm and onto his shoulder, where it settles with all its scales raised.

He feeds it from his own bowl, in the dark: a few leaves of dried plum from the tin Bai gave him, a half-spoon of honey. Pebble eats like a creature who has not eaten for twenty days, which is accurate. When it is done, it licks its claws, turns once on his shoulder and lies down against his neck. He feels its heartbeat. It is very fast and very warm.

And then, as he is lying down again, something new comes through the bond.

It is not a word. It is a shape. A feeling with edges, like a sheet of folded paper laid against the inside of his skull: crack, crack, wall, hollow, wall. He knows it at once. It is what Pebble feels when it passes through the seams of stone, the little breaks and gaps in the world that a seamwalker perceives as a map. The pangolin is showing him.

He looks at the wall beside his cot. In the dark, to his eyes, it is a plain whitewashed plaster wall. To Pebble, he realizes, it is a thing of cracks, and every crack has a direction and a depth, and behind the plaster there is a hollow, the width of a hand, where a beam has shrunk.

You can see it.

Yes, says the warm weight on his neck. Yes. This.

You are my eyes.

It is a small, dry, delighted chuckle in his head. The scales settle. Within a minute, the creature is asleep again, on his collar, with its nose in the angle of his jaw.

He lies awake for a long time with the weight of it.

* * *

He relearns to fight in the snow, behind the Pill Hall, before the bell.

There is a dead yard there, between the herb-store wall and the refuse pit, where no one comes. It is thirty paces long and ten wide, floored in beaten earth and edged with a ruin of old fence posts. It smells of ash and bark. The snow lies in a clean sheet. Jian takes off his sandals and stands in the middle of it with Pebble clinging to his collar and a stick in his hand, and tries to remember how he moved before there was a panel.

He is not good at it.

He has always used the Interface for the first move. It was a habit so deep he never noticed it: a quick look, a reading, a calculation of angle and distance, and then the body acted on the answer. Now there is no answer. There is only the stick, and a post twenty paces away, and a cold wind, and a twenty-one-year-old's reach.

He swings. He misses the post by a hand.

Again.

He sets his feet. He lets his breath out. He does what Hu taught him, in the forge, when the one-armed man would stand across the anvil and say do not look at the hammer, look at the metal: he stops trying to see the post and looks instead at the place the stick will land. He feels the space between. The wind on his cheek. The grain of the cold.

He swings. The stick cracks against the post.

He swings again, and again. By the twentieth, his arm is burning. By the fortieth, he has begun to feel the old rhythm come back, not as sight but as a kind of dumb animal certainty, a feeling in the shoulders of where a thing will be. He does it with his eyes shut. He does it with Pebble on his collar, whispering left, wall, hollow, wall, so that he steps over a fallen post he did not know was there.

It is not the Interface, he thinks, wiping sweat from his lip. It is only practice.

I should have done it from the start.

He throws pins at the post. Six, in a line. Four stick. He retrieves them and throws again. Slowly, as the days go by, the number rises to five, and then six.

* * *

The hardest part is the courtyard.

Eight boys sleep in Reed Courtyard number six, and eight boys watch each other all day, in the way boys do who have nothing else to look at. They know who stays up late. They know who has a cough. They know, within a week, that Lin Jian goes out before the bell and comes back with snow on his hair, and that he has begun to stumble on things he did not stumble on before.

"You walked into the door," says Ma Bao, on the ninth morning.

"It was dark."

"You have lived here a month. You know where the door is." Ma Bao is not being unkind; he is genuinely puzzled. "You never walk into things. You are the one who tells me when the bench is loose."

"I am tired."

"You are always tired."

"Then I am always tired." He gets up and shoulders past. "Do not stand in the way."

Pei looks at him with round worried eyes. Lan Tong, on his cot, turns his face to the wall.

He has to be careful. That is the discipline, and the cost. Every stumble is a thing to be explained. Every missed step, every dropped bowl, every moment when he does not know a plant's grade at a glance, is a thing his courtyard will remember. He wears the Veil. He wears the slow wheel. He wears, now, the clumsy awkwardness of a twenty-one-year-old who has lost something and does not know what, and he finds that it is the most convincing mask he has worn yet.

It is the first time I have been exactly what I look like.

It does not comfort him.

* * *

Feng finds him on the twelfth night, in the dead yard, practicing with the stick.

He does not announce himself. He comes round the corner of the herb-store wall in the dark, in a gray cloak, without a lantern, and stands at the edge of the snow with his arms folded. Jian does not see him until Pebble stiffens on his collar and sends a quick sharp tall, still, watching.

He lowers the stick.

"You are very slow," says Feng.

"Yes."

"You were not slow in the Garden."

"No."

"You were not slow at the ford." Feng comes forward. His limp is better; he has been taking something that Healer Song gave him, at the cost of three nights' sleep. "I watched you from the cart. You killed a man with a pin in the foot before he knew you were there. You saw him." He stops a pace away. "You were looking at the water, and you saw him, and I do not know how."

"I got lucky."

"Do not tell me you got lucky." The voice is flat and not unkind. "I have been your brother for twenty-one years. I know when you are being modest and when you are being careful, and this is the second one. You have been careful for twelve days. You walk into doors." His eyes search Jian's face in the dark. "You walked into the door on the stair, three nights after the landing. I saw you. You were standing at the thirty-ninth, and you reached for the post, and you missed it by a hand."

"It was dark."

"It was not that dark."

Jian says nothing. The wind moves in the pines. Pebble's claws tighten on his collar.

Feng takes a long breath. He looks up at the stars. When he speaks again, it is lower and slower, the voice he used in the courtyard of Green Pine Hill, on the night of the siege.

"I have not asked what you did at the landing," he says. "I do not intend to. I have thought about it a great deal, and I have decided that I do not want to know, because if I know I will have to decide what to do about it, and I have not the slightest idea what the right thing is." A faint, dry, tired smile. "I have been a first-ranker for six years. I have never once been out of my depth. It is a most unpleasant feeling."

"Feng."

"I only want to say one thing." He looks down. "Whatever it is you have lost, you have not lost the part that matters. I do not know how I know. I looked at you tonight, hitting a post in the snow with your eyes shut, and I thought: he is exactly the same boy." He steps back. "That is all. I will say nothing to anyone. Go and sleep."

He is gone before Jian can find an answer.

* * *

Elder Bai sets him the Blood Seal on the fourteenth day, and watches him fail to fail.

It is the third of the Hall's Level 1 pills, the one the steward saves for last: a dark red pill that closes wounds, made of dragon's-blood resin, Frostbell, ground carp scale and three kinds of bark. The fire is the difficulty. It must be held at the exact heat of a living body for the length of a night, never above, never below, and a boy who lets it slip by the width of a hair will find his pills clotted into a hard black pebble in the morning.

"One night," says Bai, from his stool by the bronze. "I will sit here. I will not help."

Jian lights the kettle at dusk. He feeds it a little charcoal at a time, from a bucket at his elbow, and sits cross-legged on the stone before it with his hands on his knees. Pebble is a warm lump in the front of his tunic. The furnace room is dark except for the red mouth of the fire.

He does not have the Interface. He has not had it for fourteen days. He has stumbled on steps and dropped pestles and walked into doors, and the old man has seen every stumble.

But the fire is the fire.

He looks into it and the heat opens. It is not a panel. It is not a number. It is the thing he found in the courtyard on the fourth batch, a simple animal knowledge that lives somewhere under the ribs, where the root of fire lies coiled in the pale knot of his five. The flame is a gradient and he can feel the gradient. He does not need a count or a clock. He needs only to sit and be the kind of person who knows what warm is.

Hour after hour, the fire holds.

At the second watch, Bai gets up and puts a hand on the bronze, as if to feel its pulse. He says nothing. He sits down again. At the fourth, he unwraps a paper twist of plums and eats three, slowly, without taking his eyes off the boy. At dawn, when the first gray light comes through the vent, Jian lifts the lid.

Forty-one small dark pills lie in the kettle like seeds.

Bai takes one. He bites it in half. He chews, and swallows, and for a long moment he sits quite still, with his fingers pressed to his own wrist.

"Tier low," he says. "Quality top."

Jian lets out a breath.

"Quality top. At the first attempt." The round face is expressionless. "You are aware that the last apprentice to produce a top-quality Blood Seal at the first attempt did so in the reign of the old Sect Master, and was made an Inner Sect disciple on the spot?"

"No, Elder."

"I am telling you so that you will understand what I am about to say." He puts the half-pill on the stone. "You have been clumsy for fourteen days. You drop things. You walk into doors. Ma Bao says you have forgotten how to count." The pale eyes crease. "And you have just held a fire for a night without a hair of error. Do you know what that tells me?"

"No, Elder."

"It tells me that the thing you have lost is not the thing that matters to me." Bai rises, with a grunt. "I do not wish to know what it is. I wish to know that you will survive without it." He turns toward the door. "Your trial month ends in six days. I will not stand in your way." He stops with his hand on the latch and does not turn. "One thing more." A pause, so slight that Jian would not have caught it a month ago. "When whatever it is returns, tell me whether it was worth the price. I am curious."

The door shuts. Jian sits alone in the red light with forty-one pills and a pangolin, and understands, slowly, that the old man has just told him he knows.

* * *

The stranger appears on the sixteenth day.

Jian sees him on the stair at dusk, coming back from the herb store with a bundle of dried bark under his arm. The snow has stopped. The sky is a high, thin, pale gold, the color of a pear. Below, the Court is lighting its lamps, one by one, in the blue shadow of the mountain.

He stops at the turn of the lower flight and looks across the ravine.

The Hundred Stairs has a twin. It is not the same, and few people speak of it: a narrower flight on the far side of the cleft, cut into the cliff for the use of the Medicine Valley's servants, running from the valley gate up to the herb terraces. It is a poor stair, steep and mean and unlit. On the very top of it, forty paces across the gulf from the place where Jian stands, a figure is looking at him.

It is a man, or a boy. The distance is too great to say. He wears a gray hooded cloak, pulled forward to hide the face, and he stands very straight with his hands hidden in his sleeves. He is not doing anything. He is not climbing or descending. He is simply there, in the last light, on the empty stair, with his face turned toward the Hundred Stairs and the boy who stands on them.

Pebble.

Watching, comes the thin cold answer along the bond, and then, with a small restless shiver: Old. Not-young. Stillness. The scales on Jian's collar rise. Wrong. Wrong shape.

Wrong?

Not like others. Like... a wall that walks.

Jian does not move. He holds the bundle against his side, as though it were a shield. He does not lift a hand. He does not look away. He tries, for the first time in sixteen days, to reach for the old cold clean reading of Qi and Fire and Soul, and there is nothing, only the gray line in the corner of his sight.

```
Day 16 of 30.
```

The figure on the far stair raises one hand.

It is not a wave. It is a small, deliberate gesture, palm outward, held for the space of a breath, in the way a man shows an empty hand to a creature he does not wish to alarm.

Then it lowers the hand, and turns, and goes up into the dusk.
